3.0.s.en: 1. The sweetness of the word of God:

3.0.0.en: 1 Moreover he said unto me, Son of man, eat that thou findest; eat this roll, and go speak unto the house of Israel. 2 So I opened my mouth, and he caused me to eat that roll. 3 And he said unto me, Son of man, cause thy belly to eat, and fill thy bowels with this roll that I give thee. Then did I eat it; and it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness.

3.0.1.en: The command was given to the prophet Ezekiel to eat the scroll (the word of God), as it was given to St. John the Beloved (Rev 10:9). Jeremiah says: "Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart" (Jer 15:16), and the Lord Christ says: "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God" (Mt 4:4). The word of God is a delicious food, giving life and inner joy and gladness; we are nourished by it, and so we carry it in our depths. It is sweet, even if it carries bitterness because of God's chastisements, which are for our salvation.

3.0.2.en: When the prophet Ezekiel received His word from the hands of God as an open scroll, he read what was inside it and what was outside, and found that it contained lamentations and woe together with songs of praise; so he opened his mouth for God to feed him with His own hand, and his depths were satisfied, and he found it in his mouth as honey for sweetness.

3.0.3.en: How wonderful is the love of God! He deals with us as a nurse or a tender mother, stretching out His hand to feed us, the infants beloved to Him. We throw ourselves upon His breast like a nursing child on the breast of its mother, and we find His commandment pure milk coming from His breasts (the two Testaments), like the honey of bees and the honeycomb. His commandment is suitable for the little ones and for the mature grown.

3.0.4.en: God's commandment is hard and heavy for the natural man; indeed, some sometimes see it as a fetter on human freedom. But when the hand of God is stretched out to present it to us within us, we find it sweet as honey. What is this outstretched hand (Ezek 1:9) that Ezekiel saw but the Son of God, who is called "the arm of the Lord," and who became visible through the divine Incarnation? He presented to us the divine commandment not through commands and prohibitions, but through practical mutual love between God and man, and between man and his brother, offering Himself as an example and helper, for He says: "This is my commandment, That ye love one another, as I have loved you. Ye are my friends... Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you" (Jn 14:12-15). Thus the divine commandment became not an order we are bound to obey, but the opening of our inner insight by love to perceive the will of our Beloved, so that we obey Him as beloved ones whose will meets His divine will voluntarily! By this we can understand His words: "Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me... For my yoke is easy (pleasant), and my burden is light" (Mt 11:29-30), although He had previously said: "Think not that I am come to send peace on earth: I came not to send peace, but a sword... And he that taketh not his cross, and followeth after me, is not worthy of me" (Mt 10:34, 38). By love pain becomes sweet and the cross becomes glory, and the commandment is sweet as honey.

3.0.5.en: The word of God also carries warnings against the fallen, that they may repent; these put the servant of the word in a difficult position and even expose him to troubles and afflictions, yet at the same time they offer sweetness and joy to the servant, as he realizes God's saving purposes. When the Apostle Paul wrote sternly he grieved the Corinthians, but he went on to explain to them that although they had been grieved, he rejoices in this grief which is unto repentance, so that they too rejoice with him, saying: "For if I make you sorry, who is he then that maketh me glad, but the same which is made sorry by me? And I wrote this same unto you, lest, when I came, I should have sorrow from them of whom I ought to rejoice; having confidence in you all, that my joy is the joy of you all. For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote unto you with many tears; not that ye should be grieved, but that ye might know the love which I have more abundantly unto you" (2 Cor 2:2-4).

3.1.0.en: 4 And he said unto me, Son of man, go, get thee unto the house of Israel, and speak with my words unto them. 5 For thou art not sent to a people of a strange speech and of an hard language, but to the house of Israel; 6 Not to many people of a strange speech and of an hard language, whose words thou canst not understand. Surely, had I sent thee to them, they would have hearkened unto thee. 7 But the house of Israel will not hearken unto thee; for they will not hearken unto me: for all the house of Israel are impudent and hardhearted. 8 Behold, I have made thy face strong against their faces, and thy forehead strong against their foreheads. 9 As an adamant harder than flint have I made thy forehead: fear them not, neither be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house. 10 Moreover he said unto me, Son of man, all my words that I shall speak unto thee receive in thine heart, and hear with thine ears. 11 And go, get thee to them of the captivity, unto the children of thy people, and speak unto them, and tell them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear. 12 Then the spirit took me up, and I heard behind me a voice of a great rushing, saying, Blessed be the glory of the LORD from his place. 13 I heard also the noise of the wings of the living creatures that touched one another, and the noise of the wheels over against them, and a noise of a great rushing. 14 So the spirit lifted me up, and took me away, and I went in bitterness, in the heat of my spirit; but the hand of the LORD was strong upon me.

3.1.1.en: God did not send him to foreign nations nor to a people of strange dialect, but sent him to his own people, to the nation that has the law of God. But, sadly, it was a disobedient nation that refused to listen to the law that Moses received on Mount Sinai, and continued to reject the word of God on the tongues of the prophets... until the Word Himself came, and they rejected Him.

3.2.0.en: God punishes them in an indirect way, saying to Ezekiel: "Surely, had I sent thee to them, they would have hearkened unto thee" [6]. And indeed, when the Word came, the nations of foreign race received Him.

3.3.0.en: Ezekiel's mission was exceedingly difficult, "for all the house of Israel are impudent and hardhearted" [7]. This is the effect of sin in the life of man: it makes his heart hard as stone and his forehead hard; he does not want to hear the divine voice but resists it violently without shame. But God gives His servants strength, for He says: "Behold, I have made thy face strong against their faces, and thy forehead strong against their foreheads. As an adamant harder than flint have I made thy forehead: fear them not, neither be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house" [8-9]. Though evil is violent by nature, it cannot stand to the end, for good shatters it, as light scatters darkness and truth falsehood, and the Kingdom of God remains forever while the kingdom of the devil is for a time. Thus, whenever the servant hides in God as his refuge, the enemy of good cannot stand before him.

3.4.0.en: When Ezekiel received the word of God he heard behind him a voice of a great rushing [12]; these are the heavenly powers working in secret within his heart, thundering to shatter the evil that hardened the hearts of sinners. He heard the noise of the wings of the living creatures that touched one another. It is as though the heavenly creation, which works together in one spirit, also supports us by its prayers on our behalf. As for the noise of the wheels, it is the authority of the Gospel word, which captivates hearts and draws them.

3.5.0.en: With all these resources, the divine heavenly resources and the support of the heavenly ones besides the power of the word itself, the service is full of toil and pain... The inner bitterness of heart for the sake of shattered souls is enough, for the prophet says: "So the spirit lifted me up, and took me away, and I went in bitterness, in the heat of my spirit; but the hand of the LORD was strong upon me" [14]. It is as though he were saying with the psalmist: "Despondency hath taken hold of me because of the sinners who have departed from thy law" (Ps 118).

3.5.1.en: Ezekiel had to declare the message among those who had suffered the captivity, and they had either to receive the word of God as a savour of life unto life or a savour of death unto death. Sadly, they did not benefit from the captivity, nor were their hearts softened by the chastisement, nor did they listen to the word of God in the midst of their exile, but increased in hardness and stubbornness against God and His prophets. God made clear to him that they would refuse to listen to him, and would even resist and persecute him... It is their responsibility, not his. As for him, he must enjoy a divine power that makes him hard as adamant to face their hardness [8].

3.5.2.en: The Spirit of the Lord carried him from before the throne to bring him to the captives to serve them [12-15], that he might realize that his movements are not according to his human will but according to God's plan... that he is carried by the Spirit. He came, and his soul was filled with bitterness, and the hand of the Lord was strong upon him [14]. Perhaps the secret of his soul's bitterness sprang from comparing his standing before the divine throne, sharing the praises of the heavenly ones, with his transfer to the captives, whose peace and joy of heart sin had shattered; he became embittered in his soul, saying with the Apostle Peter: "Lord, it is good for us to be here." He did not want to leave the divine throne. Perhaps he was also embittered because he felt the people's deprivation of what he had seen and experienced by standing before the divine throne!

3.6.0.en: 15 Then I came to them of the captivity at Telabib, that dwelt by the river of Chebar, and I sat where they sat, and remained there astonished among them seven days. 16 And it came to pass at the end of seven days, that the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 17 Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel: therefore hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me. 18 When I say unto the wicked, Thou shalt surely die; and thou givest him not warning, nor speakest to warn the wicked from his wicked way, to save his life; the same wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at thine hand. 19 Yet if thou warn the wicked, and he turn not from his wickedness, nor from his wicked way, he shall die in his iniquity; but thou hast delivered thy soul. 20 Again, When a righteous man doth turn from his righteousness, and commit iniquity, and I lay a stumblingblock before him, he shall die: because thou hast not given him warning, he shall die in his sin, and his righteousness which he hath done shall not be remembered; but his blood will I require at thine hand. 21 Nevertheless if thou warn the righteous man, that the righteous sin not, and he doth not sin, he shall surely live, because he is warned; also thou hast delivered thy soul.

3.7.0.en: When Ezekiel had eaten the word of God and been satisfied with it, he remained among the captives seven days in bewilderment, not knowing what to do, and the voice of the Lord came to him: "Son of man, I have made thee a watchman" [17]. It is as though two things are necessarily required for appointing the watchman: that he eat the word of God, and that he live seven days among his people. The number 7 points to perfection, or the completeness of the days of the week; it is as though the watchman is not an employee who performs a work for wages, who works for a while and rests, but truly a loving man who throws himself among his people all the days of his life, knowing no rest for himself. When the Apostle Paul wanted to describe the first leader of the people, that is, Moses the prophet, he said of him: "By faith Moses, when he was come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter; choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season; esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt: for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward" (Heb 11:24-26). Thus Moses threw himself into the disgrace of his people, counting that better than living in the comfort of Pharaoh's palace, leaving every temporary pleasure for the sake of the eternal reward. These are the marks of the spiritual watchman. He works among his people as their servant, bearing their reproach, seeking not his own but what is for their comfort.

3.7.1.en: His being called "watchman" is a sign of the existence of a spiritual war; in his service he washes the feet of others and fights Satan and his hosts.

3.7.2.en: In ancient times cities were often built on hills, and a tower was built on the city walls, and in the tower was a watchman who could track the movements of any enemy coming toward the city and warn the people; then the gates of the city were closed and the army prepared for war.

3.7.3.en: As for God's commandment to him, it is: "Hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me" [17]. As a watchman he must bear a spirit of discernment through his keeping of the word of the Lord and his fellowship with God, so that he does not warn from himself but by what he hears from the mouth of God, and does not speak in his own name but in the name of God ("from me"). By this he can warn with all strength, without fear, flattery or compromise, lest souls perish and their blood be required of him.

3.7.4.en: God made clear to His servant the extent of his responsibility for the perishing of every soul he fails to warn out of negligence, a matter that has terrified the servants of God throughout the ages. Therefore when St. Ambrose felt that the Emperor Theodosius had committed an error, he hastened to write to him warning him, saying to him: [Can I keep silent?! For my conscience would be bound, my speech taken from me, and I would be in the worst state I could be in...! If the priest does not speak with the one who sins... the sinner dies in his sin, and the priest himself is subject to punishment because he did not warn against the error]. Again he writes to him thus: [I beg you to listen patiently to what I say. If I am unworthy to be heard by you, I am also unworthy to offer sacrifices on your behalf, you who have trusted in your vows and prayers... It is not for the emperor to refuse freedom of speech, nor for the priest not to say what he thinks].

3.7.5.en: St. John Chrysostom has presented to us a wonderful example of the watchman's care not for the congregation as a whole but for each soul as if it were the whole congregation, saying: [Each one of you, in my eyes, is equal to the whole city].

3.7.6.en: Again he says: [Let no one say to me that many have fulfilled the commandment, for I do not seek this, but I want everyone to do so. I cannot catch my breath until I see that fulfilled! For if one man committed fornication among the Corinthians, Paul sighed as though the whole city were lost].

3.7.7.en: St. Paul felt his responsibility as a watchman, and he says to the presbyters of the Church in Ephesus: "Wherefore I take you to record this day, that I am pure from the blood of all men. For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God... Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears" (Acts 20:26-27, 31). And as Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles, says: [From whose blood is the Apostle pure...? The blood of souls, of course, and not the blood of bodies]. He also says: [We must fear lest the souls of many perish because of the famine of the word of God resulting from our negligence, and it be required of our souls on the day of judgment].

3.8.0.en: 22 And the hand of the LORD was there upon me; and he said unto me, Arise, go forth into the plain, and I will there talk with thee. 23 Then I arose, and went forth into the plain: and, behold, the glory of the LORD stood there, as the glory which I saw by the river of Chebar: and I fell on my face.

3.8.1.en: As he acts as a watchman, the Lord commanded him not to hasten to begin the work but to go forth into the plain to speak with him [22], and there He showed him His heavenly glory again, as he had seen by the river Chebar. For the success of the mission does not rest on the abundance of work but on the quality of the servant; he is obliged to be sanctified through his solitude with God, to lift his heart to the divine glories and so present to the people in his life "the power of the heavenly life."

3.8.2.en: Going forth into the plain to behold the glory of the Lord is necessary for every servant; therefore after the Apostle Paul was called to service he committed himself to stay three years in the wilderness in a long solitude with God to prepare for the apostolic work. St. Augustine speaks of the servants' commitment to spiritual solitude without solitude hindering the work or the work hindering the life of solitude, saying: [Those to whom works of good and the care of souls have been entrusted are obliged to bring to people a witness of the other life (contemplation); therefore they must devote themselves to the study and contemplation of the truth and of eternal life. Nor is it fair that the life of contemplation should be a cause for hindering a man from performing the tasks of the Church].

3.8.3.en: For the success of our service we need the Lord to be manifested in our hearts, and to enjoy the divine presence, not once only but from time to time, so that we enjoy continual new visions that reveal the glory of God, His power and His resources... and we are assured that He is working in us and through us. He is always present within us, manifesting Himself continually in our depths.

3.9.s.en: 5. A time to keep silence and a time to speak:

3.9.0.en: 24 Then the spirit entered into me, and set me upon my feet, and spake with me, and said unto me, Go, shut thyself within thine house. 25 But thou, O son of man, behold, they shall put bands upon thee, and shall bind thee with them, and thou shalt not go out among them: 26 And I will make thy tongue cleave to the roof of thy mouth, that thou shalt be dumb, and shalt not be to them a reprover: for they are a rebellious house. 27 But when I speak with thee, I will open thy mouth, and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; He that heareth, let him hear; and he that forbeareth, let him forbear: for they are a rebellious house.

3.9.1.en: The vision was repeated and the prophet Ezekiel's falling on his face was repeated, and the divine Spirit also entered him to raise him up and he heard this message: "Go, shut thyself within thine house... And I will make thy tongue cleave to the roof of thy mouth, that thou shalt be dumb, and shalt not be to them a reprover: for they are a rebellious house. But when I speak with thee, I will open thy mouth, and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD" [24-27]. Thus the Lord wanted him not to work by human zeal but to be silent and not speak until He permits him to speak, so that he speaks at the time the Lord sees fit and with the words of the Lord and in His name. Although as a watchman he is condemned for his silence in the face of evil, he must learn what the wise man said: "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak" (Eccl 3:7). As St. Ambrose says: [Weigh your speech and measure your words], and also: [The wise man in his speech takes into consideration what he says, to whom he speaks, and the circumstances of place and time... Thus there must be a measure for keeping silence as for speaking]. Father Gregory the Great says: [The shepherd must be discreet in his silence and profitable in his speech].

3.9.2.en: Feed me with Your commandment, O desire of my heart!

3.9.3.en: *Feed me with Your commandment, O desire of my heart!

3.9.4.en: Stretch out Your hand and give me Your commandment as heavenly bread.

3.9.5.en: I am a child, even an infant; I will not accept food from anyone but You!

3.9.6.en: You are more tender to me than my parents, O Savior of my soul!

3.9.7.en: *Your commandment is hard, O Savior of my soul, Your cross is heavy, and Your way is a narrow affliction, but from Your hands Your commandment becomes bread and honey of the bees, Your cross becomes glory, and Your way a new heaven!

3.9.8.en: *You sent Your prophet carrying Your word to Your stubborn people; grant me to carry Your commandment to every soul, however stubborn!

3.9.9.en: With the receiving of Your word a great rushing took place in heaven.

3.9.10.en: Let heaven thunder and shake every hardness in my heart and in their hearts.

3.9.11.en: Let the shaken earthly nature be removed from them, and let them enjoy an eternal heavenly life.

3.9.12.en: *Your prophet presented Your word to a stubborn people, and his soul became embittered.

3.9.13.en: Was he perhaps bitter in soul because he did not want to leave the beholding of Your chariot?!

3.9.14.en: Was he perhaps bitter in soul because he came into contact with the stubbornness of humanity?!

3.9.15.en: Grant me, in the midst of my soul's bitterness, to see Your heavens; grant me, in the midst of my sorrow, to touch the repentance of many.

3.9.16.en: My heart rejoices in Your divine work in them and through them, O divine Word.

3.9.17.en: Your prophet remained among the captives seven days; grant me to spend all the days of my exile working in Your vineyard.

3.9.18.en: I am not a hired servant counting the time, but a son who longs to work in my Father's vineyard.

3.9.20.en: When shall I be alone with You to know Your mysteries?!

3.9.21.en: And when shall I work in the vineyard to serve Your people?!

3.9.22.en: Grant me in my solitude not to forget Your people, and in my service not to cease contemplating Your mysteries.

3.9.23.en: *Guide me, O true Word, for I do not know when to be silent and when to speak, how to be silent and how to speak?!

3.9.24.en: Here I am in Your hands; be my leader who works in me.
